sections.title: Abstract

summary.text: Summarizes a pipeline for digitizing and segmenting ~831,000 scanned mathematical documents in zbMATH Open using Mathpix for LaTeX OCR and fine-tuned generative LLMs in a Majority Voting framework for document separation, achieving 97.5% text extraction accuracy (89.1% boundary index accuracy overall) and processing 810,977 documents into machine-readable text (721,288 with LaTeX boundary indexes).

sections.extract: This paper presents a specialized methodology for digitizing and segmenting mathematical documents from zbMATH Open, a com- prehensive database of mathematical literature, to enhance ma- chine processing capabilities. Currently, approximately 831,000 documents exist only in scanned volumes, which makes them not machine-processable. Furthermore, these scans often span multi- ple pages or share pages with other

sections.title: Introduction

summary.text: Introduces the problem of converting ~831,000 historical scanned review entries in zbMATH Open (out of over 4.8 million total entries) into machine-readable LaTeX for mathematical information retrieval, noting the challenges of varying historical typesetting and multi-document or multi-page scan layouts illustrated in Figure 1.

sections.extract: Introduction Printed mathematical literature has a long history, with records dating back several centuries. Among the most comprehensive re- sources in the field, zbMATH Open (1868 – present) serves as a critical abstracting and reviewing service in pure and applied math- ematics [21]. sections.title: Related Work

summary.text: Reviews prior work on post-OCR document extraction and layout segmentation using regular expressions (Pitou et al., Pandey et al.), computer vision models including Faster-RCNN, U-Net, Segmentation Transformer, and Document Image Transformer (DiT), and NLP/LLM approaches using LSTM, BERT, and GPT-3.5.

summary.text: Reports converting 254,444 scanned zbMATH Open .tiff pages via the Mathpix API into 252,209 JSON LaTeX files (with 2,235 API failures, including 1,408 blank pages and 827 recognition failures), and catalogs common OCR errors in Subsection 4.3 including character confusions, inconsistent line breaks/spacing, spurious LaTeX tags, and omitted characters or words.

sections.title: Errors analysis

summary.text: Categorizes the 12 test-set errors made by the Majority Voting method into four causes: OCR formatting errors (2 cases), ambiguity between nearly identical neighboring titles (2 cases), LLM hallucinations on longer documents (4 cases), and metadata inclusion/omission errors (4 cases).

sections.extract: Errors analysis This section reviews the main sources of errors that occur when using the Majority Voting method and analyzes each type. By do- ing this, we can better understand the limitations of the current approach and guide further optimization efforts to improve the accuracy and reliability of document-splitting methods. • OCR formatting errors: an OCR error may cause the document to be processed incorrectly

sections.title: Error detection hypotheses

summary.text: Tests and refutes two standalone error-detection hypotheses on the 18 test errors of fine-tuned CalmExperiment-7B-slerp—showing neither Mathpix page confidence scores (Hypothesis 1) nor output token probabilities from LLaMA-Factory (Hypothesis 2) reliably predict segmentation errors—and describes Subsection 8.5's whitespace-normalized exact-matching method for recovering start and end character indexes in the raw LaTeX OCR output (succeeding on 90.6% of the test set with 98.4% accuracy, or 89.1% overall while filtering out hallucinations).

sections.extract: Error detection hypotheses In addition to analyzing specific types of errors, we tested two hypotheses to identify potential indicators of errors in the document splitting process. These hypotheses focus on aspects of OCR quality and the probabilistic nature of Transformers-based Large Language Models, aiming to establish methods for error detection. sections.title: All data processing

summary.text: Reports applying the Majority Voting pipeline to all 810,977 eligible zbMATH Open documents (differing from CalmExperiment-7B-slerp alone in 3.4% of cases) and recovering exact start and end character indexes in the LaTeX scans for 721,288 documents (88.9%).

sections.extract: All data processing After achieving a high accuracy score on the test dataset, the next step was to use the best approach we had created on the entire dataset. Thus, we applied the Majority Voting approach to 810,977 elements in the zbMATH Open table, finishing the transformation of these mathematical documents into machine-readable and search- able formats as a practical outcome of this research. sections.title: Conclusion

summary.text: Concludes by summarizing the Mathpix LaTeX OCR conversion of 252,624 zbMATH Open pages, the 97.5% test accuracy of the three-LLM Majority Voting splitter (and 89.1% overall index accuracy), the public release of code, models, and datasets on GitHub, Zenodo, and Hugging Face, and DFG funding acknowledgments.

sections.extract: Conclusion This project successfully identified the optimal OCR tool, Mathpix, for converting scanned pages to LaTeX format, using the BLEU Score and Edit Distance metrics. As the next step, 252,624 scanned pages from zbMATH Open were converted into LaTeX.
